article.content_html:
Key Developments

Democratic candidate for Florida governor, David Jolly, is confronting scrutiny over his past professional ties to businessman Leo Govoni, who was indicted last year for allegedly embezzling over $100 million. The indictment, issued less than two weeks after Jolly launched his campaign, accuses Govoni of siphoning funds from a nonprofit managing assets for people with disabilities. Jolly has strongly condemned Govoni's alleged actions as "raw cruelty" and has actively distanced himself from the scandal. He clarified in a July video that he was an employee at a separate for-profit company owned by Govoni, Boston Finance Group, and that the alleged theft "appear[s] to have occurred almost exclusively after we left his employment." Jolly worked at Boston Finance Group from 2012 until early 2014, coinciding with his first successful bid for a U.S. House seat. While Jolly did not work directly for the nonprofit, federal prosecutors allege Govoni used Boston Finance Group to enrich himself. Court documents from a related case, reviewed by CBS News, indicate millions of dollars were transferred from the nonprofit to the for-profit firm during Jolly's employment period. Crucially, no court documents suggest Jolly's awareness or involvement in the scheme, and he has not been accused of any wrongdoing. He told the Tampa Bay Times he was unaware of the transfers described. Mark Riddle, a senior advisor for Jolly's campaign, affirmed Jolly has been "forthright" since learning of the matter upon Govoni's arrest. Riddle emphasized Jolly was one of over 100 W-2 employees, never an officer or in a fiduciary role, and lacked visibility into Govoni's finances. Jolly has also not been contacted by investigators nor is he a subject of the criminal investigation.

Key Takeaways

  • Florida gubernatorial candidate David Jolly is addressing his past employment with Leo Govoni, who faces charges for allegedly siphoning over $100 million from a nonprofit.
  • Jolly worked for a Govoni-owned for-profit firm where millions were reportedly transferred from the nonprofit during his employment, but he denies knowledge and involvement.
  • Jolly has not been accused of wrongdoing, contacted by investigators, or served in a fiduciary capacity for Govoni's companies.

Why It Matters

David Jolly, a former Republican now running as a Democrat, is challenging GOP Rep. Byron Donalds for the Florida governor's mansion. This controversy surrounding his former boss introduces a significant challenge to his campaign, as Florida has not elected a Democratic governor in this century. Jolly hopes that public discontent with the Republican Party could create an opportunity for him, but navigating these past ties to an alleged fraudster will be crucial in convincing voters of his integrity and suitability for office.
